newsitem.title: FRANCE: French firms face Euro stick, pensions carrot.
newsitem.headline: French firms face Euro stick, pensions carrot.

text.p: Asset allocation under the euro single currency will force French firms to focus on creating value if they are to attract international investors, speakers at a business conference said on Thursday.
Once currency risk disappears after the introduction of a single European currency, sector analyses and a tougher approach among fund managers will put the spotlight on management objectives.
Fund managers will chose "the companies most capable of creating value to repay the capital they invest," said Colette Neuville, head of the ADAM small shareholders group said.
The introduction of the euro would radically change asset allocation rules, with far-reaching implications for issuers, Monique Bourven, chairwoman of State Street Bank said.
After 1999, funds will look at sectors and value within the Euro zone instead of using country and geographical weightings tied to national currencies,

"The universe for allocation for investors, particularly international ones, after 1999 will no longer...be geographical but will become a universe of issuers," she said. Individual offerings will be scrutinised without the traditional country and currency risks.

The euro zone will represent 25 percent of world market capitalisation compared with London's current 10 percent and 40 percent in North America, 20 in Japan and 15 for the emerging markets of Asia, South America and the rest of Europe.
But a major question will be whether the euro zone will succeed in attracting more capital than other regions, she said.

For European investors, a tentative choice was already being made, with figures showing SICAV mutual funds investing in European stocks gaining 2.5 billion francs in deposits while French equity funds seeing an outflow of 6.7 billion.

Neuville, whose ADAM association specialises in representing small shareholders, cited figures from a U.S. body which showed French companies' profits had fallen 36 percent in the last five years while those of British and American firms had respectively risen 52 and 75.

The scope for improvement was attracting international investors but to maintain and increase their holdings, French companies will need to show "they can create value and create more value than their foreign competitor."
The French economy is changing to liberal capitalism from the traditional "administered capitalism" of the past decades, which sought to satisfy the demands of management and employees, she said.

But with the increasing "professionalism" of fund managers who are themselves facing greater competition for savings, companies will come under more pressure to show profitability and explain strategy and objectives.

Managers will have to demonstrate each unit's profitability and that parts of the group are not subsidising another, as well as justify acquisitions -- which have been shown to be destroyers as much as creators of value.

But French companies will get a badly-needed boost when new private pension funds are introduced, which are expected to invest heavily in shares, Jean Gandois chairman of the CNPF French employers federation said.

The French economy was hampered by a "severe lack of equity capital" but the arrival of complementary pensions would help address that gap. "We will be able to draw economic benefits for the French economy from pension funds," he said.
Banks and insurers have agreed after long-standing talks to ask that the the new funds be able to to pay out income rather than capital sums, which should make them attractive, he said.
More French equity investment was needed as shares accounted for only 22 percent of total institutional flows in the first half, while in the United States it represented almost half.

Not enough French companies are quoted and flotation procedures should be made easier, he said. France's market capitalisation was only 33 percent of the gross domestic product, whereas in the United States, it was double that and triple that in Britain.
France also needs to attract foreign investors but more company information and greater efforts to improve corporate governance were needed. "It's an essential point," he said.
